items.title: Atomic radius goes UP across the lanthanides (then drops)
items.claim: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period: protons increase but the outer shell is the same. The 4f electrons in the lanthanides screen the nucleus so poorly that radius decreases throughout the row — and then the 5d and 6s elements after them are SMALLER than expected.
items.prompt: What's the consequence of this 'lanthanide contraction'?

options.text: Elements just after the lanthanides (Hf, Ta, W and below) have surprisingly small radii, almost identical to those of the elements above them in the same group (Zr, Nb, Mo) — so zirconium and hafnium have nearly identical chemistry and are very hard to separate
Atomic radius goes UP, not down, across the lanthanides

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals, which are 'inside' the 6s shell and screen the outer electrons very poorly. So the effective nuclear charge felt by the 6s shell grows steadily — the outer shell shrinks.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72, just after the lanthanides), the atomic radius is approximately the same as zirconium (Z=40) above it. Atomic radius is 159 pm for Zr, 156 pm for Hf — virtually identical.

The practical consequence: Zr and Hf are chemically almost indistinguishable and have to be separated by very fine techniques (typically ion-exchange chromatography). They are sold side by side. Hafnium controls in nuclear reactors depend on this.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the periodic table's full structure.

items.title: Mendeleev wrote out 63 cards and left blank spaces
items.claim: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev, writing a chemistry textbook in St Petersburg, sketched out the 63 known elements ordered by atomic mass. He noticed similar properties recur periodically. Where his pattern needed an element that didn't yet exist, he LEFT A GAP and predicted the properties of the missing element.
items.prompt: Why is Mendeleev's table considered a theory rather than a classification?

options.text: Because it was published in Russia
Because it predicted unknown elements (eka-aluminium, eka-boron, eka-silicon) whose properties were measured later and matched the predictions — gallium 1875, scandium 1879, germanium 1886
Because it was written by a famous chemist
Because it was rejected by other chemists

items.reveal_title: Predictions vindicated three times in 17 years
items.reveal:
Mendeleev's 1871 predictions for eka-silicon (germanium): atomic mass ~72, density ~5.5, grey metal, oxide formula MO2.

Winkler's 1886 germanium: atomic mass 72.6, density 5.32, grey metal, GeO2.

Mendeleev had also predicted eka-aluminium (gallium, found 1875 by Lecoq de Boisbaudran) and eka-boron (scandium, found 1879 by Nilson). All three matched closely.

He was passed over for the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry — by ONE vote — in favour of Henri Moissan for isolating fluorine. He died in 1907. Element 101, mendelevium, was named in his honour in 1955.
items.why: A theory earns its keep by predicting what no one has measured. Mendeleev's table did this three times within his lifetime.

items.title: An atom of carbon-14 is chemically identical to carbon-12
items.claim: Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are all carbon. They have 6 protons and react chemically the same way. They differ only in the number of neutrons — and one of them (C-14) is radioactive.
items.prompt: Why does chemistry not distinguish isotopes?

options.text: Isotopes are too rare to matter
Chemistry is governed by the electron arrangement, which depends on the number of protons (atomic number) — neutrons add mass but do not affect the electron shells that control bonding
Isotopes are the same element with the same number of neutrons

items.reveal_title: Atomic number defines the element, mass number distinguishes isotopes
items.reveal:
Nuclide notation: write the mass number A (protons + neutrons) as a superscript and atomic number Z (protons) as a subscript before the symbol. C-14 has Z=6, A=14, so it has 8 neutrons.

Because electron configuration depends only on Z, all carbon isotopes share the same chemical behaviour. They differ in mass, nuclear stability, and very slightly in reaction rates (kinetic isotope effects — useful for mechanism studies).

C-14 is radioactive with a half-life of 5730 years and decays by beta emission to N-14. Its constant atmospheric concentration (produced by cosmic rays in the upper atmosphere) underwrites radiocarbon dating of organic remains up to about 50,000 years old.
items.why: Students often confuse isotopes with different elements. The proton count is what 'makes' the element; neutrons are bookkeeping for the nucleus.
